summary: Describes Magma, the 64-bit block cipher with a 256-bit key defined in the Russian standard GOST R 34.12-2015, alongside the 128-bit cipher Kuznyechik covered in RFC 7801. It is published to help implementers and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Magma is the 64-bit block cipher in the Russian standard GOST R 34.12-2015. This RFC explains its key schedule, encryption and decryption steps, and test examples.

subtitle: An informational description of Magma, the 64-bit block cipher in GOST R 34.12-2015.

tldr.problem: The Russian standard GOST R 34.12-2015 includes an updated 64-bit block cipher, and developers need information about its revised encryption and decryption steps.
tldr.mechanism: Magma uses a 256-bit key expanded into 32 round keys. Each round uses 4-bit substitutions, modular addition, a rotation, and an exclusive-or across the block halves.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8891 is an informational description that updates RFC 5830. It does not specify block modes, which are selected according to the protocol and its needs.

today: RFC 8891 is an Informational document published in September 2020. It updates RFC 5830, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 8891 itself.

sections.title: What Magma Describes
sections.content:
RFC 8891 describes Magma, a block cipher with a 64-bit block and a 256-bit key in GOST R 34.12-2015. The standard also includes the 128-bit cipher Kuznyechik, described in RFC 7801. The RFC presents information about the revised 64-bit cipher for developers and users.

RFC 8891 updates RFC 5830, which described the earlier GOST 28147-89 cipher. The RFC is an Independent Submission published for information; its publication statement makes no claim about implementation or deployment value.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes an updated version of a Russian block cipher. It gives implementers information about the cipher but does not recommend its use.

sections.title: Changes from the Earlier Cipher
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three clarifications or modifications compared with the earlier cipher described in RFC 5830. Magma fixes the S-box set, reads the key as one big-endian integer instead of using the earlier little-endian approach, and parses data bytes as one big-endian integer.

The document describes itself as a translation of relevant parts of GOST R 34.12-2015. It says that combining RFC 8891 with RFC 7801 provides an English translation of the standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Magma updates the earlier cipher's substitution tables and the way it reads key and data bytes. These details affect the values used during encryption.

sections.title: Substitution and Round Functions
sections.content:
Magma divides a 32-bit half into eight 4-bit pieces. Each piece passes through its corresponding substitution table, one of eight tables identified as Pi_0 through Pi_7. The round function adds a 32-bit key modulo 2^32, applies those substitutions, and rotates the result left by 11 bits.

A round then combines the transformed half with the other 32-bit half using exclusive-or and swaps their roles. The final-round function combines the halves without the same swap. Together these operations transform a 64-bit block.
sections.plainLanguage: Each round transforms one half of the block and combines it with the other half. The transformation uses fixed substitution tables, addition, and a rotation.

sections.title: The Key Schedule
sections.content:
The 256-bit key is divided into eight 32-bit words, from K_1 to K_8. The schedule repeats those words in order for the next two groups of eight round keys. It then uses the same words in reverse order for the last eight keys.

The result is 32 round keys used by the encryption and decryption procedures. The appendix includes a sample key and lists the generated round keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The key is split into eight 32-bit pieces. Magma uses the pieces in order three times, then in reverse order, to make its round keys.

sections.title: Encryption, Decryption, and Test Examples
sections.content:
Encryption applies the round function with keys K_1 through K_31, then applies the final-round function with K_32. Decryption uses the round functions with keys in reverse order and finishes with the final-round function using K_1.

Appendix A gives informative examples for the transformations, key schedule, encryption, and decryption. In its test, plaintext fedcba9876543210 encrypts to 4ee901e5c2d8ca3d, and the decryption example returns the original plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption uses 32 rounds, and decryption runs the key sequence in reverse. The RFC's test example shows the ciphertext and confirms that decryption returns the input.

sections.title: Modes and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section says the entire document is about security considerations. It also says that, unlike RFC 5830 but like RFC 7801, this specification does not define block modes for Magma. A protocol may select a mode based on its needs.

The RFC has no IANA actions. Its text describes the cipher and does not provide a separate security analysis of its strength.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines the block cipher, not how a protocol must process longer messages with it. It does not provide a separate analysis of the cipher's security strength.
